claims: I study how sea otters shape the kelp forests of Monterey Bay.
I am a PhD student in marine biology at Hopkins Marine Station in Pacific Grove.
The Nereid is forty years old and the engine fails about once a month.
Three days a week I take the research boat, the Nereid, out into Monterey Bay to count otters.
I tag juvenile otters at Elkhorn Slough and track them with radio collars for two years each.
My field site is Elkhorn Slough, a tidal estuary north of Monterey.
Sam and I co-authored a paper last year on otter foraging, and it was finally accepted in March.
Tycho is a one-eyed tabby I found injured on the dock at the marina.
My funding runs out in August.
Dr. Okafor is writing a grant to extend my stipend, but if the grant fails I will have to leave Hopkins before I finish.
I sprained my wrist last month hauling the anchor on the Nereid.
Last week we lost a tagged otter, number forty-one, to a shark bite near Elkhorn Slough.
Sam found the collar washed up on the mudflats and we were both shaken.
Dr. Okafor grew up in Lagos and came to California for graduate school, like me but a generation earlier.
The drone costs two thousand dollars
I have saved about half from teaching undergraduate labs
I back up everything to the lab server at Hopkins every night.
Tycho knocked my laptop off the desk in February and I lost a week of data analysis.
Arjun is getting married in Seattle in October.
I promised to fly up for the wedding, even though October is the worst month to leave the otter survey.
Sam and I repainted the hull ourselves over a weekend to save the lab money.
I get seasick on rough days, even after four years on the water.
I take ginger tablets before every trip on the Nereid and try not to look at the horizon.
Dr. Okafor says the data I am collecting could run for thirty years.
My dream is to start a long-term otter monitoring program at Elkhorn Slough that outlives my dissertation.
Sam pulled me out, and I have worn a life vest every day since.
I almost drowned during my first field season when I slipped off the dock at the marina in a storm.
My mother in Chennai worries that I am thirty and still in school.
I send her photos of the otters to show her that what I do is real work.
The thing I love most is the first hour on Monterey Bay at dawn, before the fog lifts, when the otters are still rafting together in the kelp.
